## The Binomial Model

The **binomial model** is a discrete-time model of a financial market in which
the price of a risky asset moves, in each period, to one of only two possible
values. Despite its simplicity it contains the main ideas of
[[option-pricing]]: replicating a payoff with a self-financing portfolio,
pricing by no arbitrage, and the risk-neutral measure. It is also easy to
compute with, handles early exercise (American options) naturally, and
converges to the [[black-scholes-merton-model]] as the time step goes to zero.

This note builds the model, shows how to price a [[derivatives|derivative]] in
it, proves [[european-options|put-call parity]], works through an example and
extends the results to a stock paying continuous dividends.

## Constructing the Model

### One Period

Consider one period of length $h$, with times $t\in\{0,h\}$, and two assets.

:::{.definition data-title="One-Period Binomial Model"}

The market consists of

- a **risk-free bond** with price $B_0=1$ and $B_h=e^{rh}$, where $r$ is the
  continuously compounded risk-free rate (see [[interest]]), and
- a **stock** with price $S_0=S$ and

  $$
  S_h =
  \begin{cases}
  uS & \text{with probability } p, \\
  dS & \text{with probability } 1-p,
  \end{cases}
  \qquad 0<d<u,
  $$

  where $u$ and $d$ are the **up** and **down factors**.

A portfolio holding $x$ bonds and $y$ shares has value
$V_t = xB_t + yS_t$.

:::

The real-world probability $p$ will play no role in pricing. The model has two
possible outcomes and two assets, which is what makes it possible to replicate
any payoff.

### No Arbitrage

:::{.theorem data-title="No Arbitrage in the Binomial Model"}

The one-period model is free of [[risk-neutral-pricing|arbitrage]] if and only
if

$$
d < e^{rh} < u.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
If $e^{rh}\le d$, borrow $S$ and buy one share. The cost at time $0$ is zero
and the value at time $h$ is $S_h - Se^{rh}$, which is at least $0$ in both
states and strictly positive in the up state, an arbitrage. If $e^{rh}\ge u$,
short one share and lend the proceeds, which is an arbitrage in the other
direction.

Conversely, suppose $d<e^{rh}<u$ and define

$$
q = \frac{e^{rh}-d}{u-d} \in (0,1).
$$

Then $q\,uS + (1-q)\,dS = e^{rh}S$, so the discounted stock price is a
martingale when the up probability is $q$. For any portfolio with zero initial
value, the discounted terminal value $e^{-rh}V_h$ therefore has expectation
$0$ under $q$. Since $q$ and $1-q$ are both positive, $V_h\ge 0$ in both states
forces $V_h=0$ in both states, so there is no arbitrage.
:::

We assume this condition from now on.

### Pricing by Replication

A derivative pays $V_u$ if the stock moves up and $V_d$ if it moves down. For a
call option with strike $K$ these are $V_u=(uS-K)^+$ and $V_d=(dS-K)^+$.

To replicate, hold $\Delta$ shares and $B$ units of cash (lent if $B>0$,
borrowed if $B<0$) so that the portfolio pays exactly the derivative in both
states,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\,uS + Be^{rh} &= V_u, \\
\Delta\,dS + Be^{rh} &= V_d.
\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the equations and solving gives

$$
\Delta = \frac{V_u - V_d}{S(u-d)},
\qquad
B = e^{-rh}\,\frac{uV_d - dV_u}{u-d}.
$$

By the no-arbitrage principle the derivative has the same price as the
replicating portfolio,

$$
V_0 = \Delta S + B.
$$

The number $\Delta$ is the **hedge ratio**: it measures how sensitive the
derivative is to the stock. A call is replicated by buying shares and
borrowing ($\Delta>0$, $B<0$), and a put by shorting shares and lending
($\Delta<0$, $B>0$). These formulas hold for any payoff $(V_u,V_d)$.

### Risk-Neutral Pricing

Substituting $\Delta$ and $B$ into $V_0=\Delta S+B$ and collecting the $V_u$
and $V_d$ terms gives

$$
V_0 = e^{-rh}\left[\,q\,V_u + (1-q)\,V_d\,\right],
\qquad
q = \frac{e^{rh}-d}{u-d}.
$$

The no-arbitrage condition $d<e^{rh}<u$ is exactly the condition $0<q<1$. The
number $q$ is the **risk-neutral probability** of an up move. It is not the
real-world probability $p$. It is the probability under which the stock earns
the risk-free rate on average,

$$
e^{-rh}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[S_h] = S,
$$

so the price of the derivative is its discounted expected payoff under the
risk-neutral measure $\mathbb{Q}$, as in [[risk-neutral-pricing]]. Replication
and risk-neutral expectation give the same price because the second is
derived from the first.

### Multiple Periods

Divide $[0,T]$ into $n$ periods of length $h=T/n$. In each period the stock
moves up by $u$ or down by $d$, independently of the past, so after $j$ up
moves and $k-j$ down moves at time $kh$ the price is $S u^j d^{k-j}$. The tree
**recombines**: an up move followed by a down move ends at the same price as a
down move followed by an up move, so there are only $k+1$ nodes at time $kh$.

Prices are found by **backward induction**:

1. At maturity set the node value equal to the payoff $h(S_T)$.
2. At each earlier node apply the one-period formulas to the two values that
   follow it,

   $$
   V = e^{-rh}\left[\,q\,V_{\text{up}} + (1-q)\,V_{\text{down}}\,\right].
   $$

3. Repeat until time $0$.

Since $u$, $d$ and $r$ do not change, $q$ is the same at every node. The hedge
$\Delta$ and the cash position $B$ do change from node to node, so the
replicating portfolio is **rebalanced** at each node. The rebalancing is
self-financing: the portfolio held coming into a node is worth exactly the
cost of the new portfolio.

Unrolling the recursion gives a closed form.

:::{.theorem data-title="Multi-Period Binomial Price"}

A European derivative with payoff $h(S_T)$ has time-$0$ price

$$
V_0 = e^{-rT}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}\,q^{\,j}(1-q)^{n-j}\,
h\!\left(S u^{j}d^{\,n-j}\right).
$$

:::

This is the discounted expectation of $h(S_T)$ when the number of up moves is
$\text{Binomial}(n,q)$. At every node the discounted stock price
$e^{-rkh}S_{kh}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-martingale (see [[martingale-theory]]).

### Choosing $u$ and $d$

The factors $u$ and $d$ are model parameters. To match a stock with volatility
$\sigma$ the **Cox-Ross-Rubinstein (CRR)** choice is

$$
u = e^{\sigma\sqrt{h}},
\qquad
d = \frac{1}{u} = e^{-\sigma\sqrt{h}}.
$$

The no-arbitrage condition $d<e^{rh}<u$ holds for small enough $h$. As
$n\to\infty$ the binomial price of a European option converges to its
Black-Scholes price (see [[european-options]]), because the log-return over
$[0,T]$ is a sum of $n$ independent steps and tends to a normal distribution
by the central limit theorem.

## Put-Call Parity

:::{.theorem data-title="Put-Call Parity"}

In the binomial model, a European call and put with the same strike $K$ and
maturity $T$ on a stock paying no dividends have prices satisfying

$$
C_0 - P_0 = S_0 - Ke^{-rT}.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
The payoffs satisfy, in every state,

$$
(S_T-K)^+ - (K-S_T)^+ = S_T - K.
$$

By the pricing formula above, which is linear in the payoff,

$$
C_0 - P_0 = e^{-rT}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}\left[(S_T-K)^+ - (K-S_T)^+\right]
= e^{-rT}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[S_T - K].
$$

Since $e^{-rt}S_t$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-martingale, $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[S_T]
= e^{rT}S_0$, hence

$$
C_0 - P_0 = e^{-rT}\left(e^{rT}S_0 - K\right) = S_0 - Ke^{-rT}.
\qquad\blacksquare
$$
:::

The parity can also be seen from replication in one period. The call and put
have values $(uS-K)^+$, $(dS-K)^+$ and $(K-uS)^+$, $(K-dS)^+$, and their
difference $C-P$ has value $uS-K$ in the up state and $dS-K$ in the down
state. Applying the replication formulas with $V_u=uS-K$ and $V_d=dS-K$,

$$
\Delta_C-\Delta_P = \frac{(uS-K)-(dS-K)}{S(u-d)} = 1,
\qquad
B_C-B_P = e^{-rh}\,\frac{u(dS-K)-d(uS-K)}{u-d} = -Ke^{-rh},
$$

so $C-P=S-Ke^{-rh}$. A long call and short put therefore replicate a long
share financed by borrowing $Ke^{-rh}$, which is a forward contract. Note
that the proof uses only the no-arbitrage condition, not the values of $u$
and $d$ or the real-world probability $p$. The parity holds at every node of
the tree, with $S$ and the remaining time to maturity taken at that node.

## Example

Price a European call and put on a stock with $S_0=100$, strike $K=100$,
maturity $T=1$ and rate $r=5\%$, using $n=2$ periods ($h=0.5$) with $u=1.2$ and
$d=0.85$.

**Parameters.** $e^{rh}=e^{0.025}=1.025315$, so $d<e^{rh}<u$ and there is no
arbitrage. The risk-neutral probability and discount factor are

$$
q = \frac{1.025315-0.85}{1.2-0.85} = 0.500900,
\qquad
e^{-rh} = 0.975310.
$$

**Stock tree.** $S_u=120$, $S_d=85$, $S_{uu}=144$, $S_{ud}=102$ and
$S_{dd}=72.25$.

**Terminal payoffs.**

| Node | $S_T$ | Call $(S_T-100)^+$ | Put $(100-S_T)^+$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| $uu$ | 144 | 44 | 0 |
| $ud$ | 102 | 2 | 0 |
| $dd$ | 72.25 | 0 | 27.75 |

**Backward induction.** Applying $V=e^{-rh}[qV_{\text{up}}+(1-q)V_{\text{down}}]$:

| Node | $S$ | Call $C$ | Put $P$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| $u$ | 120 | 22.4690 | 0.0000 |
| $d$ | 85 | 0.9771 | 13.5081 |
| root | 100 | 11.4525 | 6.5754 |

For example, the call at the root is
$C_0 = 0.975310\,[\,0.5009(22.4690)+0.4991(0.9771)\,] = 11.4525$.

**Hedge at the root (call).** With $V_u=22.4690$ and $V_d=0.9771$,

$$
\Delta = \frac{22.4690-0.9771}{100(0.35)} = 0.6141,
\qquad
B = 0.975310\cdot\frac{1.2(0.9771)-0.85(22.4690)}{0.35} = -49.9531,
$$

and indeed $\Delta S+B = 61.41-49.95 = 11.4525$. To replicate the call, buy
$0.6141$ shares and borrow $\$49.95$.

**Put-call parity check.**

$$
C_0-P_0 = 11.4525-6.5754 = 4.8771,
\qquad
S_0-Ke^{-rT} = 100-100e^{-0.05} = 4.8771. \;\checkmark
$$

## Continuous Dividends

Suppose the stock pays dividends continuously at a constant yield $\delta$,
which are reinvested in the stock. Then $\Delta$ shares held at time $0$ grow
to $\Delta e^{\delta h}$ shares at time $h$. The model is otherwise the same,
and every result above carries over with $r$ replaced by $r-\delta$ in the
stock's drift.

**No arbitrage.** The model is free of arbitrage if and only if

$$
d < e^{(r-\delta)h} < u.
$$

The proof is the same as before, comparing the stock with the bond after
reinvesting dividends.

**Replication.** The replicating portfolio must satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\,uS\,e^{\delta h} + Be^{rh} &= V_u, \\
\Delta\,dS\,e^{\delta h} + Be^{rh} &= V_d,
\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\Delta = e^{-\delta h}\,\frac{V_u - V_d}{S(u-d)},
\qquad
B = e^{-rh}\,\frac{uV_d - dV_u}{u-d},
\qquad
V_0 = \Delta S + B.
$$

**Risk-neutral pricing.** Substituting gives

$$
V_0 = e^{-rh}\left[\,q\,V_u + (1-q)\,V_d\,\right],
\qquad
q = \frac{e^{(r-\delta)h}-d}{u-d}.
$$

The no-arbitrage condition is again $0<q<1$. Under $q$ the stock has expected
growth $e^{(r-\delta)h}$ per period, so the stock with its dividends reinvested
earns the risk-free rate, $e^{-rt}e^{\delta t}S_t$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-martingale,
and $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[S_T] = e^{(r-\delta)T}S_0$.

**Multiple periods.** Backward induction uses the new $q$ and the new
$\Delta$ at each node, and the closed form is unchanged,

$$
V_0 = e^{-rT}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}\,q^{\,j}(1-q)^{n-j}\,
h\!\left(S u^{j}d^{\,n-j}\right).
$$

For the CRR tree $u=e^{\sigma\sqrt{h}}$, $d=1/u$, the condition
$d<e^{(r-\delta)h}<u$ again holds for small $h$.

:::{.theorem data-title="Put-Call Parity with Dividends"}

For a stock paying a continuous dividend yield $\delta$,

$$
C_0 - P_0 = S_0e^{-\delta T} - Ke^{-rT}.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
As before, $(S_T-K)^+ - (K-S_T)^+ = S_T-K$, so by linearity
$C_0-P_0 = e^{-rT}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[S_T-K]$. Using
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{Q}}[S_T]=e^{(r-\delta)T}S_0$,

$$
C_0 - P_0 = e^{-rT}\left(e^{(r-\delta)T}S_0 - K\right)
= S_0e^{-\delta T} - Ke^{-rT}.
\qquad\blacksquare
$$
:::

In one period the replication formulas with $V_u=uS-K$ and $V_d=dS-K$ give
$\Delta_C-\Delta_P=e^{-\delta h}$ and $B_C-B_P=-Ke^{-rh}$, so a long call and
short put replicate a forward contract on the stock with reinvested dividends,
financed by borrowing $Ke^{-rh}$.

An option on an exchange rate fits this framework, with $S$ the exchange rate
in domestic currency per unit of foreign currency and $\delta$ the foreign
interest rate, since a unit of foreign currency held in a foreign bank account
grows at that rate.

## Extensions

- **American options.** The holder may exercise at any node, so backward
  induction takes the larger of the exercise value and the continuation value,

  $$
  V = \max\left(\text{payoff},\;
  e^{-rh}\left[\,q\,V_{\text{up}} + (1-q)\,V_{\text{down}}\,\right]\right),
  $$

  where $V_{\text{up}}$ and $V_{\text{down}}$ are themselves American values.
  An American call on a stock with no dividends is never exercised early, but
  an American put can be, as can a call when $\delta>0$ is large. Parity then
  holds only as an inequality.
- **Other payoffs.** The same tree prices any path-independent payoff, and
  with extra bookkeeping path-dependent options such as
  [[barrier-options]].
